themes.name: Incentives Before Standards
themes.plain: Many of these problems stall because the person or company holding the answer gains nothing by sharing it, and no one can make them. The blockers are money and politics, inside the company as much as outside, so the models try to make honesty or cooperation pay rather than write another rule.
themes.evidence: On the shared meaning layer all three models called conflicting definitions of customer a political fight over whose number changes, and the same logic shows up in agent traffic (offering fast lanes and better prices to agents that declare themselves), journey orchestration (channel owners paid for sends resisting suppression), and incrementality (platforms with no reason to expose how treatment was assigned).

themes.name: Judgment That Won't Compile
themes.plain: The hardest calls turn on meaning and context: whether a picture plus a headline implies a promise, whether evidence really backs a claim, whether two teams can both be right about what a word means. No rule set captures that, so the models shrink human judgment into a smaller, safer box instead of removing it.
themes.evidence: On content governance the models restrict generation to pre-approved claims because implied meaning cannot be checked automatically, and on the shared meaning layer they argue that legitimate competing definitions must be disclosed rather than collapsed into one right answer.

themes.name: No Ground Truth to Measure Against
themes.plain: Most of these problems have no answer key. There is no stable number to grade your work against, and the thing being measured often moves while you measure it, so the models start by building a small truth set of their own or admit the number is only an estimate.
themes.evidence: Answer engine work begins with a fixed panel of real buyer questions because model drift swamps any change you make, identity matching needs a recruited panel of consenting people to grade matches, incrementality needs standing holdout markets, and B2B intent has almost no accounts that ever buy to learn from.

themes.name: Nobody Can Verify Downstream
themes.plain: Once data, a message, or a dollar leaves your own systems, you cannot see inside the partner, ad platform, or trained model that now holds it. You can watch from outside and estimate whether the rules were followed, but you cannot prove it.
themes.evidence: On downstream consent the models fall back to expiring audience feeds, signed evidence that the signal was sent, and planted canary identities, and all three say a person cannot be pulled back out of a model already trained on them.

themes.name: Chokepoint Before Trust
themes.plain: When the models cannot trust who is acting or what will happen next, they build one door they own and push everything through it. A sent email, a spent dollar, or an exported file cannot be taken back, so the only real control happens before the action leaves.
themes.evidence: Safe agent execution draws the same answer from all three models (a proxy or gateway holding the credentials, with hard spend, rate, and audience caps), downstream consent gets a single checkpoint on every data exit, and orchestration gets one shared contact log every channel must check before sending.
